Day 29: Month 1 Project Day 2 — Twitter Clone Implementation Build the tweet and feed services Month 1: Foundations › Week 4: Communication Patterns Tags: Theory JavaScript Python Estimated Time: 90–120 minutes 📖 Theory What You'll Learn Today Today we explore Month 1 Project Day 2 — Twitter Clone Implementation — a fundamental concept you'll encounter when designing large-scale systems. Understanding this well is the difference between a system that breaks under load and one that scales gracefully. Core Topics Tweet Service Fan-out Service Timeline Cache User Service Search Integration WebSocket Notifications Why It Matters Month 1 Project Day 2 — Twitter Clone Implementation is used in production systems at Google, Netflix, Uber, and Amazon. The concepts you learn today appear in system design interviews and every day in engineering work. The key engineering mindset: every design decision is a trade-off . There is no perfect solution — only the best solution for your specific requirements, scale, and constraints. Deep Dive Deep Dive: Fan-Out on Write vs Fan-Out on Read Fan-out on write (push): When User A posts, immediately write the tweet ID to Redis timeline lists for all followers. Reading a timeline is O(1) — just return the pre-cached list. Cost: one tweet for a user with 10M followers = 10M Redis writes. With active celebrities, write infrastructure melts. Fan-out on read (pull): No writes on post. When a user opens their feed, fetch the list of 500 people they follow, run 500 DB queries, merge and sort. Every timeline load = 500+ queries. At 100M DAU × 10 loads/day = 500 billion DB queries/day. Impossible. The hybrid (Twitter's actual approach): - Regular users (< ~1M followers): fan-out on write. Tweets pushed to all followers' Redis timeline caches. - Celebrities (explicitly flagged): no fan-out on write. - Timeline assembly: return pre-cached tweet IDs + live-fetch recent celebrity tweets + merge by timestamp. This means most timeline content is O(1) from Redis, plus a small live fetch for the ~10–30 celebrities any user might follow. Still very fast, avoids catastrophic write amplification for celebrity posts. 🍎 Real-World Analogy Real-World Analogy: A School's Personalised Morning Bulletin Every student gets a morning bulletin showing posts from teachers they follow and classmate news. Fan-out on write (pre-printed personalised bulletin): When a teacher posts at 8pm, the printing office immediately adds it to every subscribed student's bulletin. Student arrives at 7am — their bulletin is already assembled. Instant read. But: the principal has 2,000 subscribers. Every principal post triggers 2,000 bulletin additions simultaneously. Fan-out on read (assemble on demand): No pre-printing. When a student arrives, they walk to each of their 30 teachers' noticeboards, collect today's posts, and assemble their own bulletin. 30 trips × 2 minutes = 60 minutes of assembly. Unusable. The hybrid: Pre-print bulletins for regular teachers (fan-out on write — manageable print volume). For high-profile staff (principal, department heads) with 500+ subscribers: don't pre-print. When a student's bulletin is assembled, live-fetch the principal's recent posts and insert them at the top. The concepts you learn today appear in system design interviews and every day in engineering work. The key engineering mindset: every design decision is a trade-off . docs.text: Fan-out on write (push): When User A posts, immediately write the tweet ID to Redis timeline lists for all followers. Reading a timeline is O(1) — just return the pre-cached list. Cost: one tweet for a user with 10M followers = 10M Redis writes. With active celebrities, write infrastructure melts. Fan-out on read (pull): No writes on post. When a user opens their feed, fetch the list of 500 people they follow, run 500 DB queries, merge and sort. Every timeline load = 500+ queries. At 100M DAU × 10 loads/day = 500 billion DB queries/day. Impossible. The hybrid (Twitter's actual approach): - Regular users (< ~1M followers): fan-out on write. Tweets pushed to all followers' Redis timeline caches. - Celebrities (explicitly flagged): no fan-out on write. - Timeline assembly: return pre-cached tweet IDs + live-fetch recent celebrity tweets + merge by timestamp. This means most timeline content is O(1) from Redis, plus a small live fetch for the ~10–30 celebrities any user might follow. Still very fast, avoids catastrophic write amplification for celebrity posts.
docs.title: Deep Dive: Fan-Out on Write vs Fan-Out on Read

docs.text: Every student gets a morning bulletin showing posts from teachers they follow and classmate news. Fan-out on write (pre-printed personalised bulletin): When a teacher posts at 8pm, the printing office immediately adds it to every subscribed student's bulletin. Student arrives at 7am — their bulletin is already assembled. Instant read. But: the principal has 2,000 subscribers. Every principal post triggers 2,000 bulletin additions simultaneously. Fan-out on read (assemble on demand): No pre-printing. When a student arrives, they walk to each of their 30 teachers' noticeboards, collect today's posts, and assemble their own bulletin. 30 trips × 2 minutes = 60 minutes of assembly. Unusable. The hybrid: Pre-print bulletins for regular teachers (fan-out on write — manageable print volume). For high-profile staff (principal, department heads) with 500+ subscribers: don't pre-print. When a student's bulletin is assembled, live-fetch the principal's recent posts and insert them at the top. Students get their personalised pre-assembled content instantly, plus the principal's current posts added in a second quick pass.

Day 31: Authentication with JWT and OAuth Proving who you are to a system Month 2: Security and Architecture › Week 5: Security Essentials Tags: Theory JavaScript Python Estimated Time: 90–120 minutes 📖 Theory What You'll Learn Today Today we explore Authentication with JWT and OAuth — a fundamental concept you'll encounter when designing large-scale systems. Understanding this well is the difference between a system that breaks under load and one that scales gracefully. Core Topics Session Tokens JWT Structure JWT Signing OAuth2 Flow Refresh Tokens PKCE Single Sign-On Cookie vs Token Why It Matters Authentication with JWT and OAuth is used in production systems at Google, Netflix, Uber, and Amazon. The concepts you learn today appear in system design interviews and every day in engineering work. The key engineering mindset: every design decision is a trade-off . There is no perfect solution — only the best solution for your specific requirements, scale, and constraints. Deep Dive Let's break down each core topic: Session Tokens : This is the foundation. Without understanding this, the rest doesn't make sense. Take your time here. JWT Structure : Once you have the foundation, this builds on top of it. Day 33: Advanced Rate Limiting Protecting APIs from abuse and bots Month 2: Security and Architecture › Week 5: Security Essentials Tags: Theory JavaScript Python Estimated Time: 90–120 minutes 📖 Theory What You'll Learn Today Today we explore Advanced Rate Limiting — a fundamental concept you'll encounter when designing large-scale systems. Understanding this well is the difference between a system that breaks under load and one that scales gracefully. Core Topics Token Bucket Algorithm Leaky Bucket Fixed Window Sliding Window Distributed Rate Limiting Redis Counter API Keys Why It Matters Advanced Rate Limiting is used in production systems at Google, Netflix, Uber, and Amazon. The concepts you learn today appear in system design interviews and every day in engineering work. The key engineering mindset: every design decision is a trade-off . There is no perfect solution — only the best solution for your specific requirements, scale, and constraints. Deep Dive Let's break down each core topic: Token Bucket Algorithm : This is the foundation. Without understanding this, the rest doesn't make sense. Take your time here. Leaky Bucket : Once you have the foundation, this builds on top of it. You'll see this in almost every real-world system. Fixed Window : This is where the real engineering happens. Companies spend months optimising this. Common Mistakes to Avoid Over-engineering early : Don't add complexity before you need it Ignoring the trade-offs : Every choice has costs — acknowledge them Not estimating first : Always estimate scale before choosing a design Forgetting failure modes : What happens when each component fails? 🍎 Real-World Analogy Think of Advanced Rate Limiting like how a large airport operates: - Multiple runways handle traffic (parallel processing) - Control tower coordinates everything (orchestration) - Backup systems activate if something fails (redundancy) - Everything is monitored in real time (observability) Good system design follows the same principles as good infrastructure design: plan for failure, design for scale, and keep things simple where possible. 🔑 Key Concepts Token Bucket Algorithm Leaky Bucket Fixed Window Sliding Window Distributed Rate Limiting Redis Counter API Keys 💛 JavaScript Example // Day 33: Advanced Rate Limiting // ============================================================ // Practical JavaScript implementation demonstrating: // Token Bucket Algorithm, Leaky Bucket, Fixed Window class AdvancedRateLimitingDemo { constructor(config = {}) { this.config = { maxRetries: 3, timeout: 5000, ...config }; this.stats = { requests: 0, successes: 0, failures: 0, latencyTotal: 0 }; console.log(`🚀 Advanced Rate Limiting Demo initialized`); console.log(` Config: ${JSON.stringify(this.config)}`); } // Core operation async execute(input) { const start = Date.now(); this.stats.requests++; try { const result = await this._process(input); this.stats.successes++; this.stats.latencyTotal += Date.now() - start; return { success: true, data: result, latency: Date.now() - start }; } catch (error) { this.stats.failures++; console.error(`❌ Error processing ${input}: ${error.message}`); return { success: false, error: error.message }; } } async _process(input) { // Simulate some processing time await new Promise(r => setTimeout(r, Math.random() * 50)); // Core logic representing Token Bucket Algorithm return { input, processed: true, result: `result_of_${input}` }; } // Show statistics getStats() { const avgLatency = this.stats.requests > 0 ? (this.stats.latencyTotal / this.stats.requests).toFixed(2) : 0; return { ...this.stats, successRate: `${((this.stats.successes / (this.stats.requests || 1)) * 100).toFixed(1)}%`, avgLatencyMs: avgLatency }; } } // ── Demo ────────────────────────────────────────────────────── async function runDemo() { const demo = new AdvancedRateLimitingDemo(); console.log('
📊 Running 5 sample operations...'); const inputs = ['request_A', 'request_B', 'request_C', 'request_D', 'request_E']; const results = await Promise.all(inputs.map(i => demo.execute(i))); results.forEach((r, i) => { const icon = r.success ? '✅' : '❌'; console.log(` ${icon} ${inputs[i]}: ${r.success ? `${r.data.result} (${r.latency}ms)` : r.error}`); }); console.log('
📈 Final Statistics:'); console.log(demo.getStats()); } runDemo(); 🐍 Python Example # Day 33: Advanced Rate Limiting # ============================================================ # Practical Python implementation demonstrating: # Token Bucket Algorithm, Leaky Bucket, Fixed Window import time import random import threading from dataclasses import dataclass, field from typing import Any, Dict, List, Optional @dataclass class OperationResult: success: bool data: Any = None error: str = None latency_ms: float = 0.0 class AdvancedRateLimitingSystem: # Implementation of Advanced Rate Limiting concepts # Demonstrates: Token Bucket Algorithm, Leaky Bucket, Fixed Window def __init__(self, config: Dict = None): self.config = config or {'max_retries': 3, 'timeout': 5.0} self.stats = {'requests': 0, 'successes': 0, 'failures': 0, 'total_latency': 0.0} self._lock = threading.Lock() print(f"🚀 Advanced Rate Limiting System initialized") print(f" Config: {self.config}") def execute(self, input_data: Any) -> OperationResult: # Process a single operation with metrics tracking start = time.time() with self._lock: self.stats['requests'] += 1 try: result = self._process(input_data) latency = (time.time() - start) * 1000 with self._lock: self.stats['successes'] += 1 self.stats['total_latency'] += latency return OperationResult(success=True, data=result, latency_ms=round(latency, 2)) except Exception as e: with self._lock: self.stats['failures'] += 1 return OperationResult(success=False, error=str(e)) def _process(self, input_data: Any) -> Any: # Simulate processing (replace with real implementation) time.sleep(random.uniform(0.01, 0.05)) return {'input': input_data, 'processed': True, 'output': f'result_of_{input_data}'} def get_stats(self) -> Dict: with self._lock: total = self.stats['requests'] avg_latency = self.stats['total_latency'] / total if total > 0 else 0 return { **self.stats, 'success_rate': f"{self.stats['successes'] / max(total, 1) * 100:.1f}%", 'avg_latency_ms': f"{avg_latency:.2f}ms" } def run_demo(): system = AdvancedRateLimitingSystem() print('
📊 Running 5 sample operations...') inputs = ['request_A', 'request_B', 'request_C', 'request_D', 'request_E'] for inp in inputs: result = system.execute(inp) if result.success: print(f" ✅ {inp}: {result.data['output']} ({result.latency_ms}ms)") else: print(f" ❌ {inp}: {result.error}") print('
📈 Final Statistics:') for k, v in system.get_stats().items(): print(f" {k}: {v}") if __name__ == '__main__': run_demo() 📝 Homework Research : Find a real engineering blog post about Token Bucket Algorithm (try engineering.atscale.com, netflixtechblog.com, or engineering.fb.com) Code Challenge : Extend the example above to log every operation to a file with timestamps Design Exercise : Draw a system diagram showing how Advanced Rate Limiting fits into a ride-sharing app like Uber Trade-off Analysis : What are 3 situations where you would NOT use this approach? start) * 1000 with self._lock: self.stats['successes'] += 1 self.stats['total_latency'] += latency return OperationResult(success=True, data=result, latency_ms=round(latency, 2)) except Exception as e: with self._lock: self.stats['failures'] += 1 return OperationResult(success=False, error=str(e)) def _process(self, input_data: Any) -> Any: # Simulate processing (replace with real implementation) time.sleep(random.uniform(0.01, 0.05)) return {'input': input_data, 'processed': True, 'output': f'result_of_{input_data}'} def get_stats(self) -> Dict: with self._lock: total = self.stats['requests'] avg_latency = self.stats['total_latency'] / total if total > 0 else 0 return { **self.stats, 'success_rate': f"{self.stats['successes'] / max(total, 1) * 100:.1f}%", 'avg_latency_ms': f"{avg_latency:.2f}ms" } def run_demo(): system = MonolithvsMicroservicesSystem() print('\n📊 Running 5 sample operations...') inputs = ['request_A', 'request_B', 'request_C', 'request_D', 'request_E'] for inp in inputs: result = system.execute(inp) if result.success: print(f" ✅ {inp}: {result.data['output']} ({result.latency_ms}ms)") else: print(f" ❌ {inp}: {result.error}") print('\n📈 Final Statistics:') for k, v in system.get_stats().items(): print(f" {k}: {v}") if __name__ == '__main__': run_demo()

start) * 1000 with self._lock: self.stats['successes'] += 1 self.stats['total_latency'] += latency return OperationResult(success=True, data=result, latency_ms=round(latency, 2)) except Exception as e: with self._lock: self.stats['failures'] += 1 return OperationResult(success=False, error=str(e)) def _process(self, input_data: Any) -> Any: # Simulate processing (replace with real implementation) time.sleep(random.uniform(0.01, 0.05)) return {'input': input_data, 'processed': True, 'output': f'result_of_{input_data}'} def get_stats(self) -> Dict: with self._lock: total = self.stats['requests'] avg_latency = self.stats['total_latency'] / total if total > 0 else 0 return { **self.stats, 'success_rate': f"{self.stats['successes'] / max(total, 1) * 100:.1f}%", 'avg_latency_ms': f"{avg_latency:.2f}ms" } def run_demo(): system = CircuitBreakerPatternSystem() print('\n📊 Running 5 sample operations...') inputs = ['request_A', 'request_B', 'request_C', 'request_D', 'request_E'] for inp in inputs: result = system.execute(inp) if result.success: print(f" ✅ {inp}: {result.data['output']} ({result.latency_ms}ms)") else: print(f" ❌ {inp}: {result.error}") print('\n📈 Final Statistics:') for k, v in system.get_stats().items(): print(f" {k}: {v}") if __name__ == '__main__': run_demo()

docs.text: # Day 42: API Versioning # ============================================================ # Practical Python implementation demonstrating: # URL Versioning, Header Versioning, Backward Compatibility import time import random import threading from dataclasses import dataclass, field from typing import Any, Dict, List, Optional @dataclass class OperationResult: success: bool data: Any = None error: str = None latency_ms: float = 0.0 class APIVersioningSystem: # Implementation of API Versioning concepts # Demonstrates: URL Versioning, Header Versioning, Backward Compatibility def __init__(self, config: Dict = None): self.config = config or {'max_retries': 3, 'timeout': 5.0} self.stats = {'requests': 0, 'successes': 0, 'failures': 0, 'total_latency': 0.0} self._lock = threading.Lock() print(f"🚀 API Versioning System initialized") print(f" Config: {self.config}") def execute(self, input_data: Any) -> OperationResult: # Process a single operation with metrics tracking start = time.time() with self._lock: self.stats['requests'] += 1 try: result = self._process(input_data) latency = (time.time() - start) * 1000 with self._lock: self.stats['successes'] += 1 self.stats['total_latency'] += latency return OperationResult(success=True, data=result, latency_ms=round(latency, 2)) except Exception as e: with self._lock: self.stats['failures'] += 1 return OperationResult(success=False, error=str(e)) def _process(self, input_data: Any) -> Any: # Simulate processing (replace with real implementation) time.sleep(random.uniform(0.01, 0.05)) return {'input': input_data, 'processed': True, 'output': f'result_of_{input_data}'} def get_stats(self) -> Dict: with self._lock: total = self.stats['requests'] avg_latency = self.stats['total_latency'] / total if total > 0 else 0 return { **self.stats, 'success_rate': f"{self.stats['successes'] / max(total, 1) * 100:.1f}%", 'avg_latency_ms': f"{avg_latency:.2f}ms" } def run_demo(): system = APIVersioningSystem() print('\n📊 Running 5 sample operations...') inputs = ['request_A', 'request_B', 'request_C', 'request_D', 'request_E'] for inp in inputs: result = system.execute(inp) if result.success: print(f" ✅ {inp}: {result.data['output']} ({result.latency_ms}ms)") else: print(f" ❌ {inp}: {result.error}") print('\n📈 Final Statistics:') for k, v in system.get_stats().items(): print(f" {k}: {v}") if __name__ == '__main__': run_demo()

start) * 1000 with self._lock: self.stats['successes'] += 1 self.stats['total_latency'] += latency return OperationResult(success=True, data=result, latency_ms=round(latency, 2)) except Exception as e: with self._lock: self.stats['failures'] += 1 return OperationResult(success=False, error=str(e)) def _process(self, input_data: Any) -> Any: # Simulate processing (replace with real implementation) time.sleep(random.uniform(0.01, 0.05)) return {'input': input_data, 'processed': True, 'output': f'result_of_{input_data}'} def get_stats(self) -> Dict: with self._lock: total = self.stats['requests'] avg_latency = self.stats['total_latency'] / total if total > 0 else 0 return { **self.stats, 'success_rate': f"{self.stats['successes'] / max(total, 1) * 100:.1f}%", 'avg_latency_ms': f"{avg_latency:.2f}ms" } def run_demo(): system = Week6ProjectMicroserviceChatAppSystem() print('\n📊 Running 5 sample operations...') inputs = ['request_A', 'request_B', 'request_C', 'request_D', 'request_E'] for inp in inputs: result = system.execute(inp) if result.success: print(f" ✅ {inp}: {result.data['output']} ({result.latency_ms}ms)") else: print(f" ❌ {inp}: {result.error}") print('\n📈 Final Statistics:') for k, v in system.get_stats().items(): print(f" {k}: {v}") if __name__ == '__main__': run_demo()

Understanding this well is the difference between a system that breaks under load and one that scales gracefully. Core Topics AWS S3 Bucket Policies Presigned URLs Storage Classes Lifecycle Rules Multipart Upload Versioning Event Notifications Why It Matters Object Storage is used in production systems at Google, Netflix, Uber, and Amazon. The concepts you learn today appear in system design interviews and every day in engineering work. The key engineering mindset: every design decision is a trade-off . There is no perfect solution — only the best solution for your specific requirements, scale, and constraints. Deep Dive Let's break down each core topic: AWS S3 : This is the foundation. Without understanding this, the rest doesn't make sense. Take your time here. Bucket Policies : Once you have the foundation, this builds on top of it. You'll see this in almost every real-world system. Presigned URLs : This is where the real engineering happens. Companies spend months optimising this. Common Mistakes to Avoid Over-engineering early : Don't add complexity before you need it Ignoring the trade-offs : Every choice has costs — acknowledge them Not estimating first : Always estimate scale before choosing a design Forgetting failure modes : What happens when each component fails? 🍎 Real-World Analogy Think of Object Storage like how a large airport operates: - Multiple runways handle traffic (parallel processing) - Control tower coordinates everything (orchestration) - Backup systems activate if something fails (redundancy) - Everything is monitored in real time (observability) Good system design follows the same principles as good infrastructure design: plan for failure, design for scale, and keep things simple where possible. 🔑 Key Concepts AWS S3 Bucket Policies Presigned URLs Storage Classes Lifecycle Rules Multipart Upload Versioning Event Notifications 💛 JavaScript Example // Day 52: Object Storage // ============================================================ // Practical JavaScript implementation demonstrating: // AWS S3, Bucket Policies, Presigned URLs class ObjectStorageDemo { constructor(config = {}) { this.config = { maxRetries: 3, timeout: 5000, ...config }; this.stats = { requests: 0, successes: 0, failures: 0, latencyTotal: 0 }; console.log(`🚀 Object Storage Demo initialized`); console.log(` Config: ${JSON.stringify(this.config)}`); } // Core operation async execute(input) { const start = Date.now(); this.stats.requests++; try { const result = await this._process(input); this.stats.successes++; this.stats.latencyTotal += Date.now() - start; return { success: true, data: result, latency: Date.now() - start }; } catch (error) { this.stats.failures++; console.error(`❌ Error processing ${input}: ${error.message}`); return { success: false, error: error.message }; } } async _process(input) { // Simulate some processing time await new Promise(r => setTimeout(r, Math.random() * 50)); // Core logic representing AWS S3 return { input, processed: true, result: `result_of_${input}` }; } // Show statistics getStats() { const avgLatency = this.stats.requests > 0 ? (this.stats.latencyTotal / this.stats.requests).toFixed(2) : 0; return { ...this.stats, successRate: `${((this.stats.successes / (this.stats.requests || 1)) * 100).toFixed(1)}%`, avgLatencyMs: avgLatency }; } } // ── Demo ────────────────────────────────────────────────────── async function runDemo() { const demo = new ObjectStorageDemo(); console.log('

'✅' : '❌'; console.log(` ${icon} ${inputs[i]}: ${r.success ? `${r.data.result} (${r.latency}ms)` : r.error}`); }); console.log('
📈 Final Statistics:'); console.log(demo.getStats()); } runDemo(); 🐍 Python Example # Day 52: Object Storage # ============================================================ # Practical Python implementation demonstrating: # AWS S3, Bucket Policies, Presigned URLs import time import random import threading from dataclasses import dataclass, field from typing import Any, Dict, List, Optional @dataclass class OperationResult: success: bool data: Any = None error: str = None latency_ms: float = 0.0 class ObjectStorageSystem: # Implementation of Object Storage concepts # Demonstrates: AWS S3, Bucket Policies, Presigned URLs def __init__(self, config: Dict = None): self.config = config or {'max_retries': 3, 'timeout': 5.0} self.stats = {'requests': 0, 'successes': 0, 'failures': 0, 'total_latency': 0.0} self._lock = threading.Lock() print(f"🚀 Object Storage System initialized") print(f" Config: {self.config}") def execute(self, input_data: Any) -> OperationResult: # Process a single operation with metrics tracking start = time.time() with self._lock: self.stats['requests'] += 1 try: result = self._process(input_data) latency = (time.time() - start) * 1000 with self._lock: self.stats['successes'] += 1 self.stats['total_latency'] += latency return OperationResult(success=True, data=result, latency_ms=round(latency, 2)) except Exception as e: with self._lock: self.stats['failures'] += 1 return OperationResult(success=False, error=str(e)) def _process(self, input_data: Any) -> Any: # Simulate processing (replace with real implementation) time.sleep(random.uniform(0.01, 0.05)) return {'input': input_data, 'processed': True, 'output': f'result_of_{input_data}'} def get_stats(self) -> Dict: with self._lock: total = self.stats['requests'] avg_latency = self.stats['total_latency'] / total if total > 0 else 0 return { **self.stats, 'success_rate': f"{self.stats['successes'] / max(total, 1) * 100:.1f}%", 'avg_latency_ms': f"{avg_latency:.2f}ms" } def run_demo(): system = ObjectStorageSystem() print('

Day 54: Data Warehousing Analytics at scale with columnar storage Month 2: Security and Architecture › Week 8: Advanced Storage Tags: Theory JavaScript Python Estimated Time: 90–120 minutes 📖 Theory What You'll Learn Today Today we explore Data Warehousing — a fundamental concept you'll encounter when designing large-scale systems. Understanding this well is the difference between a system that breaks under load and one that scales gracefully. Core Topics OLAP vs OLTP Star Schema Snowflake Schema Fact Tables Dimension Tables BigQuery Redshift Partitioning Clustering Why It Matters Data Warehousing is used in production systems at Google, Netflix, Uber, and Amazon. The concepts you learn today appear in system design interviews and every day in engineering work. The key engineering mindset: every design decision is a trade-off . There is no perfect solution — only the best solution for your specific requirements, scale, and constraints. Deep Dive Let's break down each core topic: OLAP vs OLTP : This is the foundation. Without understanding this, the rest doesn't make sense. Take your time here. Star Schema : Once you have the foundation, this builds on top of it. You'll see this in almost every real-world system. Snowflake Schema : This is where the real engineering happens. Companies spend months optimising this. Common Mistakes to Avoid Over-engineering early : Don't add complexity before you need it Ignoring the trade-offs : Every choice has costs — acknowledge them Not estimating first : Always estimate scale before choosing a design Forgetting failure modes : What happens when each component fails? 🍎 Real-World Analogy Think of Data Warehousing like how a large airport operates: - Multiple runways handle traffic (parallel processing) - Control tower coordinates everything (orchestration) - Backup systems activate if something fails (redundancy) - Everything is monitored in real time (observability) Good system design follows the same principles as good infrastructure design: plan for failure, design for scale, and keep things simple where possible. 🔑 Key Concepts OLAP vs OLTP Star Schema Snowflake Schema Fact Tables Dimension Tables BigQuery Redshift Partitioning Clustering 💛 JavaScript Example // Day 54: Data Warehousing // ============================================================ // Practical JavaScript implementation demonstrating: // OLAP vs OLTP, Star Schema, Snowflake Schema class DataWarehousingDemo { constructor(config = {}) { this.config = { maxRetries: 3, timeout: 5000, ...config }; this.stats = { requests: 0, successes: 0, failures: 0, latencyTotal: 0 }; console.log(`🚀 Data Warehousing Demo initialized`); console.log(` Config: ${JSON.stringify(this.config)}`); } // Core operation async execute(input) { const start = Date.now(); this.stats.requests++; try { const result = await this._process(input); this.stats.successes++; this.stats.latencyTotal += Date.now() - start; return { success: true, data: result, latency: Date.now() - start }; } catch (error) { this.stats.failures++; console.error(`❌ Error processing ${input}: ${error.message}`); return { success: false, error: error.message }; } } async _process(input) { // Simulate some processing time await new Promise(r => setTimeout(r, Math.random() * 50)); // Core logic representing OLAP vs OLTP return { input, processed: true, result: `result_of_${input}` }; } // Show statistics getStats() { const avgLatency = this.stats.requests > 0 ? (this.stats.latencyTotal / this.stats.requests).toFixed(2) : 0; return { ...this.stats, successRate: `${((this.stats.successes / (this.stats.requests || 1)) * 100).toFixed(1)}%`, avgLatencyMs: avgLatency }; } } // ── Demo ────────────────────────────────────────────────────── async function runDemo() { const demo = new DataWarehousingDemo(); console.log('

'✅' : '❌'; console.log(` ${icon} ${inputs[i]}: ${r.success ? `${r.data.result} (${r.latency}ms)` : r.error}`); }); console.log('
📈 Final Statistics:'); console.log(demo.getStats()); } runDemo(); 🐍 Python Example # Day 54: Data Warehousing # ============================================================ # Practical Python implementation demonstrating: # OLAP vs OLTP, Star Schema, Snowflake Schema import time import random import threading from dataclasses import dataclass, field from typing import Any, Dict, List, Optional @dataclass class OperationResult: success: bool data: Any = None error: str = None latency_ms: float = 0.0 class DataWarehousingSystem: # Implementation of Data Warehousing concepts # Demonstrates: OLAP vs OLTP, Star Schema, Snowflake Schema def __init__(self, config: Dict = None): self.config = config or {'max_retries': 3, 'timeout': 5.0} self.stats = {'requests': 0, 'successes': 0, 'failures': 0, 'total_latency': 0.0} self._lock = threading.Lock() print(f"🚀 Data Warehousing System initialized") print(f" Config: {self.config}") def execute(self, input_data: Any) -> OperationResult: # Process a single operation with metrics tracking start = time.time() with self._lock: self.stats['requests'] += 1 try: result = self._process(input_data) latency = (time.time() - start) * 1000 with self._lock: self.stats['successes'] += 1 self.stats['total_latency'] += latency return OperationResult(success=True, data=result, latency_ms=round(latency, 2)) except Exception as e: with self._lock: self.stats['failures'] += 1 return OperationResult(success=False, error=str(e)) def _process(self, input_data: Any) -> Any: # Simulate processing (replace with real implementation) time.sleep(random.uniform(0.01, 0.05)) return {'input': input_data, 'processed': True, 'output': f'result_of_{input_data}'} def get_stats(self) -> Dict: with self._lock: total = self.stats['requests'] avg_latency = self.stats['total_latency'] / total if total > 0 else 0 return { **self.stats, 'success_rate': f"{self.stats['successes'] / max(total, 1) * 100:.1f}%", 'avg_latency_ms': f"{avg_latency:.2f}ms" } def run_demo(): system = DataWarehousingSystem() print('

📈 Final Statistics:') for k, v in system.get_stats().items(): print(f" {k}: {v}") if __name__ == '__main__': run_demo() 📝 Homework Research : Find a real engineering blog post about OLAP vs OLTP (try engineering.atscale.com, netflixtechblog.com, or engineering.fb.com) Code Challenge : Extend the example above to log every operation to a file with timestamps Design Exercise : Draw a system diagram showing how Data Warehousing fits into a ride-sharing app like Uber Trade-off Analysis : What are 3 situations where you would NOT use this approach? start) * 1000 with self._lock: self.stats['successes'] += 1 self.stats['total_latency'] += latency return OperationResult(success=True, data=result, latency_ms=round(latency, 2)) except Exception as e: with self._lock: self.stats['failures'] += 1 return OperationResult(success=False, error=str(e)) def _process(self, input_data: Any) -> Any: # Simulate processing (replace with real implementation) time.sleep(random.uniform(0.01, 0.05)) return {'input': input_data, 'processed': True, 'output': f'result_of_{input_data}'} def get_stats(self) -> Dict: with self._lock: total = self.stats['requests'] avg_latency = self.stats['total_latency'] / total if total > 0 else 0 return { **self.stats, 'success_rate': f"{self.stats['successes'] / max(total, 1) * 100:.1f}%", 'avg_latency_ms': f"{avg_latency:.2f}ms" } def run_demo(): system = ColumnOrientedDatabasesSystem() print('\n📊 Running 5 sample operations...') inputs = ['request_A', 'request_B', 'request_C', 'request_D', 'request_E'] for inp in inputs: result = system.execute(inp) if result.success: print(f" ✅ {inp}: {result.data['output']} ({result.latency_ms}ms)") else: print(f" ❌ {inp}: {result.error}") print('\n📈 Final Statistics:') for k, v in system.get_stats().items(): print(f" {k}: {v}") if __name__ == '__main__': run_demo()

Day 56: Time-Series Databases Storing and querying metrics and events over time Month 2: Security and Architecture › Week 8: Advanced Storage Tags: Theory JavaScript Python Estimated Time: 90–120 minutes 📖 Theory What You'll Learn Today Today we explore Time-Series Databases — a fundamental concept you'll encounter when designing large-scale systems. Understanding this well is the difference between a system that breaks under load and one that scales gracefully. Core Topics InfluxDB Prometheus TimescaleDB Downsampling Retention Policies Cardinality Write-Optimised Storage Aggregation Why It Matters Time-Series Databases is used in production systems at Google, Netflix, Uber, and Amazon. The concepts you learn today appear in system design interviews and every day in engineering work. The key engineering mindset: every design decision is a trade-off . There is no perfect solution — only the best solution for your specific requirements, scale, and constraints. Deep Dive Let's break down each core topic: InfluxDB : This is the foundation. start) * 1000 with self._lock: self.stats['successes'] += 1 self.stats['total_latency'] += latency return OperationResult(success=True, data=result, latency_ms=round(latency, 2)) except Exception as e: with self._lock: self.stats['failures'] += 1 return OperationResult(success=False, error=str(e)) def _process(self, input_data: Any) -> Any: # Simulate processing (replace with real implementation) time.sleep(random.uniform(0.01, 0.05)) return {'input': input_data, 'processed': True, 'output': f'result_of_{input_data}'} def get_stats(self) -> Dict: with self._lock: total = self.stats['requests'] avg_latency = self.stats['total_latency'] / total if total > 0 else 0 return { **self.stats, 'success_rate': f"{self.stats['successes'] / max(total, 1) * 100:.1f}%", 'avg_latency_ms': f"{avg_latency:.2f}ms" } def run_demo(): system = FullTextSearchwithElasticsearchSystem() print('\n📊 Running 5 sample operations...') inputs = ['request_A', 'request_B', 'request_C', 'request_D', 'request_E'] for inp in inputs: result = system.execute(inp) if result.success: print(f" ✅ {inp}: {result.data['output']} ({result.latency_ms}ms)") else: print(f" ❌ {inp}: {result.error}") print('\n📈 Final Statistics:') for k, v in system.get_stats().items(): print(f" {k}: {v}") if __name__ == '__main__': run_demo()

start) * 1000 with self._lock: self.stats['successes'] += 1 self.stats['total_latency'] += latency return OperationResult(success=True, data=result, latency_ms=round(latency, 2)) except Exception as e: with self._lock: self.stats['failures'] += 1 return OperationResult(success=False, error=str(e)) def _process(self, input_data: Any) -> Any: # Simulate processing (replace with real implementation) time.sleep(random.uniform(0.01, 0.05)) return {'input': input_data, 'processed': True, 'output': f'result_of_{input_data}'} def get_stats(self) -> Dict: with self._lock: total = self.stats['requests'] avg_latency = self.stats['total_latency'] / total if total > 0 else 0 return { **self.stats, 'success_rate': f"{self.stats['successes'] / max(total, 1) * 100:.1f}%", 'avg_latency_ms': f"{avg_latency:.2f}ms" } def run_demo(): system = Month2ProjectDay2OrdersandPaymentsSystem() print('\n📊 Running 5 sample operations...') inputs = ['request_A', 'request_B', 'request_C', 'request_D', 'request_E'] for inp in inputs: result = system.execute(inp) if result.success: print(f" ✅ {inp}: {result.data['output']} ({result.latency_ms}ms)") else: print(f" ❌ {inp}: {result.error}") print('\n📈 Final Statistics:') for k, v in system.get_stats().items(): print(f" {k}: {v}") if __name__ == '__main__': run_demo()

start) * 1000 with self._lock: self.stats['successes'] += 1 self.stats['total_latency'] += latency return OperationResult(success=True, data=result, latency_ms=round(latency, 2)) except Exception as e: with self._lock: self.stats['failures'] += 1 return OperationResult(success=False, error=str(e)) def _process(self, input_data: Any) -> Any: # Simulate processing (replace with real implementation) time.sleep(random.uniform(0.01, 0.05)) return {'input': input_data, 'processed': True, 'output': f'result_of_{input_data}'} def get_stats(self) -> Dict: with self._lock: total = self.stats['requests'] avg_latency = self.stats['total_latency'] / total if total > 0 else 0 return { **self.stats, 'success_rate': f"{self.stats['successes'] / max(total, 1) * 100:.1f}%", 'avg_latency_ms': f"{avg_latency:.2f}ms" } def run_demo(): system = DesignaSearchEngineSystem() print('\n📊 Running 5 sample operations...') inputs = ['request_A', 'request_B', 'request_C', 'request_D', 'request_E'] for inp in inputs: result = system.execute(inp) if result.success: print(f" ✅ {inp}: {result.data['output']} ({result.latency_ms}ms)") else: print(f" ❌ {inp}: {result.error}") print('\n📈 Final Statistics:') for k, v in system.get_stats().items(): print(f" {k}: {v}") if __name__ == '__main__': run_demo()

start) * 1000 with self._lock: self.stats['successes'] += 1 self.stats['total_latency'] += latency return OperationResult(success=True, data=result, latency_ms=round(latency, 2)) except Exception as e: with self._lock: self.stats['failures'] += 1 return OperationResult(success=False, error=str(e)) def _process(self, input_data: Any) -> Any: # Simulate processing (replace with real implementation) time.sleep(random.uniform(0.01, 0.05)) return {'input': input_data, 'processed': True, 'output': f'result_of_{input_data}'} def get_stats(self) -> Dict: with self._lock: total = self.stats['requests'] avg_latency = self.stats['total_latency'] / total if total > 0 else 0 return { **self.stats, 'success_rate': f"{self.stats['successes'] / max(total, 1) * 100:.1f}%", 'avg_latency_ms': f"{avg_latency:.2f}ms" } def run_demo(): system = DesignUberRideSharingSystem() print('\n📊 Running 5 sample operations...') inputs = ['request_A', 'request_B', 'request_C', 'request_D', 'request_E'] for inp in inputs: result = system.execute(inp) if result.success: print(f" ✅ {inp}: {result.data['output']} ({result.latency_ms}ms)") else: print(f" ❌ {inp}: {result.error}") print('\n📈 Final Statistics:') for k, v in system.get_stats().items(): print(f" {k}: {v}") if __name__ == '__main__': run_demo()

Understanding this well is the difference between a system that breaks under load and one that scales gracefully. Core Topics Idempotency Keys Double-Spend Prevention Saga Pattern Reconciliation PCI-DSS Compliance Fraud Detection Why It Matters Design a Payment System is used in production systems at Google, Netflix, Uber, and Amazon. The concepts you learn today appear in system design interviews and every day in engineering work. The key engineering mindset: every design decision is a trade-off . There is no perfect solution — only the best solution for your specific requirements, scale, and constraints. Deep Dive Let's break down each core topic: Idempotency Keys : This is the foundation. Without understanding this, the rest doesn't make sense. Take your time here. Double-Spend Prevention : Once you have the foundation, this builds on top of it. You'll see this in almost every real-world system. Saga Pattern : This is where the real engineering happens. Companies spend months optimising this. Common Mistakes to Avoid Over-engineering early : Don't add complexity before you need it Ignoring the trade-offs : Every choice has costs — acknowledge them Not estimating first : Always estimate scale before choosing a design Forgetting failure modes : What happens when each component fails? 🍎 Real-World Analogy Think of Design a Payment System like how a large airport operates: - Multiple runways handle traffic (parallel processing) - Control tower coordinates everything (orchestration) - Backup systems activate if something fails (redundancy) - Everything is monitored in real time (observability) Good system design follows the same principles as good infrastructure design: plan for failure, design for scale, and keep things simple where possible. 🔑 Key Concepts Idempotency Keys Double-Spend Prevention Saga Pattern Reconciliation PCI-DSS Compliance Fraud Detection 💛 JavaScript Example // Day 80: Design a Payment System // ============================================================ // Practical JavaScript implementation demonstrating: // Idempotency Keys, Double-Spend Prevention, Saga Pattern class DesignaPaymentSystemDemo { constructor(config = {}) { this.config = { maxRetries: 3, timeout: 5000, ...config }; this.stats = { requests: 0, successes: 0, failures: 0, latencyTotal: 0 }; console.log(`🚀 Design a Payment System Demo initialized`); console.log(` Config: ${JSON.stringify(this.config)}`); } // Core operation async execute(input) { const start = Date.now(); this.stats.requests++; try { const result = await this._process(input); this.stats.successes++; this.stats.latencyTotal += Date.now() - start; return { success: true, data: result, latency: Date.now() - start }; } catch (error) { this.stats.failures++; console.error(`❌ Error processing ${input}: ${error.message}`); return { success: false, error: error.message }; } } async _process(input) { // Simulate some processing time await new Promise(r => setTimeout(r, Math.random() * 50)); // Core logic representing Idempotency Keys return { input, processed: true, result: `result_of_${input}` }; } // Show statistics getStats() { const avgLatency = this.stats.requests > 0 ? (this.stats.latencyTotal / this.stats.requests).toFixed(2) : 0; return { ...this.stats, successRate: `${((this.stats.successes / (this.stats.requests || 1)) * 100).toFixed(1)}%`, avgLatencyMs: avgLatency }; } } // ── Demo ────────────────────────────────────────────────────── async function runDemo() { const demo = new DesignaPaymentSystemDemo(); console.log('
📊 Running 5 sample operations...'); const inputs = ['request_A', 'request_B', 'request_C', 'request_D', 'request_E']; const results = await Promise.all(inputs.map(i => demo.execute(i))); results.forEach((r, i) => { const icon = r.success ? '✅' : '❌'; console.log(` ${icon} ${inputs[i]}: ${r.success ? `${r.data.result} (${r.latency}ms)` : r.error}`); }); console.log('
📈 Final Statistics:'); console.log(demo.getStats()); } runDemo(); 🐍 Python Example # Day 80: Design a Payment System # ============================================================ # Practical Python implementation demonstrating: # Idempotency Keys, Double-Spend Prevention, Saga Pattern import time import random import threading from dataclasses import dataclass, field from typing import Any, Dict, List, Optional @dataclass class OperationResult: success: bool data: Any = None error: str = None latency_ms: float = 0.0 class DesignaPaymentSystemSystem: # Implementation of Design a Payment System concepts # Demonstrates: Idempotency Keys, Double-Spend Prevention, Saga Pattern def __init__(self, config: Dict = None): self.config = config or {'max_retries': 3, 'timeout': 5.0} self.stats = {'requests': 0, 'successes': 0, 'failures': 0, 'total_latency': 0.0} self._lock = threading.Lock() print(f"🚀 Design a Payment System System initialized") print(f" Config: {self.config}") def execute(self, input_data: Any) -> OperationResult: # Process a single operation with metrics tracking start = time.time() with self._lock: self.stats['requests'] += 1 try: result = self._process(input_data) latency = (time.time() - start) * 1000 with self._lock: self.stats['successes'] += 1 self.stats['total_latency'] += latency return OperationResult(success=True, data=result, latency_ms=round(latency, 2)) except Exception as e: with self._lock: self.stats['failures'] += 1 return OperationResult(success=False, error=str(e)) def _process(self, input_data: Any) -> Any: # Simulate processing (replace with real implementation) time.sleep(random.uniform(0.01, 0.05)) return {'input': input_data, 'processed': True, 'output': f'result_of_{input_data}'} def get_stats(self) -> Dict: with self._lock: total = self.stats['requests'] avg_latency = self.stats['total_latency'] / total if total > 0 else 0 return { **self.stats, 'success_rate': f"{self.stats['successes'] / max(total, 1) * 100:.1f}%", 'avg_latency_ms': f"{avg_latency:.2f}ms" } def run_demo(): system = DesignaPaymentSystemSystem() print('
📊 Running 5 sample operations...') inputs = ['request_A', 'request_B', 'request_C', 'request_D', 'request_E'] for inp in inputs: result = system.execute(inp) if result.success: print(f" ✅ {inp}: {result.data['output']} ({result.latency_ms}ms)") else: print(f" ❌ {inp}: {result.error}") print('
📈 Final Statistics:') for k, v in system.get_stats().items(): print(f" {k}: {v}") if __name__ == '__main__': run_demo() 📝 Homework Research : Find a real engineering blog post about Idempotency Keys (try engineering.atscale.com, netflixtechblog.com, or engineering.fb.com) Code Challenge : Extend the example above to log every operation to a file with timestamps Design Exercise : Draw a system diagram showing how Design a Payment System fits into a ride-sharing app like Uber Trade-off Analysis : What are 3 situations where you would NOT use this approach? docs.text: # Day 89: Mock Interview 3 — Social Media Feed # ============================================================ # Practical Python implementation demonstrating: # Fan-out Strategy Decision, Celebrity Problem Solution, Cache Invalidation import time import random import threading from dataclasses import dataclass, field from typing import Any, Dict, List, Optional @dataclass class OperationResult: success: bool data: Any = None error: str = None latency_ms: float = 0.0 class MockInterview3SocialMediaFeedSystem: # Implementation of Mock Interview 3 — Social Media Feed concepts # Demonstrates: Fan-out Strategy Decision, Celebrity Problem Solution, Cache Invalidation def __init__(self, config: Dict = None): self.config = config or {'max_retries': 3, 'timeout': 5.0} self.stats = {'requests': 0, 'successes': 0, 'failures': 0, 'total_latency': 0.0} self._lock = threading.Lock() print(f"🚀 Mock Interview 3 — Social Media Feed System initialized") print(f" Config: {self.config}") def execute(self, input_data: Any) -> OperationResult: # Process a single operation with metrics tracking start = time.time() with self._lock: self.stats['requests'] += 1 try: result = self._process(input_data) latency = (time.time() - start) * 1000 with self._lock: self.stats['successes'] += 1 self.stats['total_latency'] += latency return OperationResult(success=True, data=result, latency_ms=round(latency, 2)) except Exception as e: with self._lock: self.stats['failures'] += 1 return OperationResult(success=False, error=str(e)) def _process(self, input_data: Any) -> Any: # Simulate processing (replace with real implementation) time.sleep(random.uniform(0.01, 0.05)) return {'input': input_data, 'processed': True, 'output': f'result_of_{input_data}'} def get_stats(self) -> Dict: with self._lock: total = self.stats['requests'] avg_latency = self.stats['total_latency'] / total if total > 0 else 0 return { **self.stats, 'success_rate': f"{self.stats['successes'] / max(total, 1) * 100:.1f}%", 'avg_latency_ms': f"{avg_latency:.2f}ms" } def run_demo(): system = MockInterview3SocialMediaFeedSystem() print('\n📊 Running 5 sample operations...') inputs = ['request_A', 'request_B', 'request_C', 'request_D', 'request_E'] for inp in inputs: result = system.execute(inp) if result.success: print(f" ✅ {inp}: {result.data['output']} ({result.latency_ms}ms)") else: print(f" ❌ {inp}: {result.error}") print('\n📈 Final Statistics:') for k, v in system.get_stats().items(): print(f" {k}: {v}") if __name__ == '__main__': run_demo()
